VERDICT: ACCEPT

The final answer N is correct under the standard fixed-query, zero-error (Las Vegas) model. The proposed justification is weak, though, and one of its claims is false.

**Why N is correct.** Upper bound: the classical deterministic algorithm that queries one point per index, N queries in all, identifies g with certainty, so Q_LV(B_N) ≤ N.

Lower bound: take k < N parallel queries with ancilla, so the final state for oracle g is ψ_g = ρ(g)^{⊗k}ψ on W⊗A. Zero-error identification with positive success probability needs the vectors {ψ_g} to be linearly independent, since a zero-error POVM element E_g satisfies ⟨ψ_h|E_g|ψ_h⟩ = 0 for h ≠ g. Because the family is G-symmetric, this independence would hold for all g or fail for all g. Independence would need the orbit span to have dimension |G|, which requires every irreducible to occur in W⊗A.

Such a component is missing when k < N. Irreps (∅, μ) with μ ⊢ N have the sign subgroup {±1}^N acting by the character ∏s_i. A point orbit of k < N points leaves some index i unhit, and the sign flip at i lies in the stabilizer and acts by −1 on (∅, μ). So (∅, μ) has no fixed vector under any stabilizer and does not occur in (C^{2N})^{⊗k}. Hence no zero-error algorithm with fewer than N queries succeeds with positive probability, and Q_LV(B_N) ≥ N.

**Problems with the proposed reasoning.** The claim that "for transitive permutation group actions, quantum queries cannot improve over the classical base size" is false in general. Bounded-error quantum identification can beat the base size for some groups, including symmetric groups. The argument for B_N only works because of the zero-error requirement, which the write-up never mentions. The base-size argument for the classical case is fine, but it does not establish the quantum lower bound.

**Caveat.** I assumed the standard fixed-k definition with parallel queries, and I relied on parallel queries being optimal in this symmetric setting. An expected-query definition with adaptive stopping could in principle give a different value, and I did not check that case.

CONFIDENCE: 3
